concepts.def: The smallest unit of life; carries out the functions needed to live.
A cell with a nucleus enclosed in a membrane; e.g. animal, plant, fungus cells.
A smaller cell with no nucleus; DNA is a loop in the cytoplasm; e.g. bacteria.
Parts inside a cell with specific jobs: nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes, chloroplasts.
Cells adapted for a specific role, e.g. red blood cell, sperm, root hair.
Undifferentiated cell that can divide to form many cell types.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Organisation of the Organism — a core area of GCSE Biology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Organisation of the Organism brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Organisation of the Organism.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Can sucrose move in both directions in the phloem?
options: Yes — translocation goes from any source (e.g. leaves) to any sink (e.g. roots, fruits), so direction varies seasonally and between phloem sieve tubes.
Phloem always carries sucrose downwards from leaves to roots.
Phloem carries water upwards and sucrose downwards in the same tube.
Decomposers turn dead matter into oxygen and water, with no carbon involved.

mcqs.q: How do decomposers return carbon to the atmosphere?
options: They respire — breaking down dead organic matter and releasing CO2.
Phloem carries water upwards and sucrose downwards in the same tube.
Decomposers turn dead matter into oxygen and water, with no carbon involved.
Decomposers release carbon by physically breaking matter into smaller pieces.
Decomposers turn dead matter into oxygen and water, with no carbon involved.
One daughter molecule contains both original strands; the other contains both new strands.
Each new DNA molecule contains one original (parental) strand and one newly synthesised strand.
DNA replication produces two identical fully new molecules with no original material.
